prompt: Two vectors of 300 random numbers (each drawn independently from a bell curve around 0) are compared by the cosine of the angle between them, which runs from −1-1−1 (opposite) through 0 (perpendicular) to 1 (same direction). What is a typical value?

options.html: Around 0.5: random arrows are about halfway similar.
Around ±0.06\pm 0.06±0.06: random arrows in 300 dimensions are almost perpendicular.
Around ±0.7\pm 0.7±0.7, as in two dimensions.

explain: About ±0.06\pm 0.06±0.06, which is 1/3001/\sqrt{300}1/300​. In two dimensions random arrows point anywhere, and the cosine is spread over the whole range. In 300 dimensions, a random arrow spreads its length over directions the other arrow barely uses, so their cosine is tiny. That is why a cosine of 0.6 between two embeddings is a strong signal: chance alone almost never produces it. M34 proves this concentration.

Can the dot product of two unit vectors in 1,000 dimensions exceed 1?

options.html: No: by Cauchy-Schwarz it is at most ∥x∥ ∥y∥=1\|x\|\,\|y\| = 1∥x∥∥y∥=1, with equality only when the vectors are the same.

explain: No. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it by the product of the lengths, in every dimension, and equality needs the vectors to be parallel. In floating point a computed cosine can come out as 1.00000000000000021.00000000000000021.0000000000000002 for parallel vectors, which is why code clips it before calling arccos; the mathematics is not to blame.

Computing 100,000 cosine similarities in a Python loop versus one NumPy matrix-vector product: roughly how much faster is NumPy?

options.html: No faster: the arithmetic is the same.

explain: Typically 100 times or more. The arithmetic is identical, but a Python loop pays for interpreting every operation and every number, while NumPy runs one compiled loop over contiguous memory. Vectorizing is the first and largest optimization in numerical Python; the GPU lessons apply the same idea once more, with thousands of cores.

prompt: What does a dot product measure, and why does it need normalizing to compare directions?
answer: x . y = |x| |y| cos(angle): it measures how far the two arrows point the same way, scaled by both lengths. A long vector has a large dot product with almost anything, so to compare directions alone divide by the lengths, giving the cosine similarity between -1 and 1.
